channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: [26] Effectiveness of Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Post-Stroke Depressive Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials With Subgroup Analyses of Standard and Adapted Approaches.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 randomized controlled trials (n=994) examined whether cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) reduces post-stroke depressive symptoms and whether adapted CBT outperforms standard CBT.
FINDINGS: CBT reduced depressive symptoms versus control (SMD −1.00, 95 % CI −1.61 to −0.39, p=0.001; I²=95 %). Subgroup analyses suggested adapted CBT was effective (SMD −1.16, 95 % CI −1.92 to −0.40, p=0.003; I²=94 %), whereas standard CBT was not (SMD −0.58, 95 % CI −1.52 to 0.36, p=0.23; I²=93 %). The test for subgroup differences was non-significant (p=0.35).
INTERPRETATION: The pooled effect favours CBT overall, but the very high heterogeneity and non-significant subgroup difference mean we cannot conclude that adapted CBT is superior to standard CBT. Risk of bias and inconsistent intervention delivery across studies further limit certainty. Larger, rigorously controlled RCTs with standardized CBT protocols are needed before firm recommendations can be made.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence suggests CBT may help post-stroke depression, but the magnitude and best delivery format remain uncertain; clinicians should monitor individual response and consider adapted formats when cognitive demands are high.

item.title: [19] Efficacy of Digital Health Interventions for Insomnia: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Insomnia is prevalent and access to first-line treatments is limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis of 44 RCTs (n=10,521) evaluated the efficacy of digital health interventions (DHIs) across eight sleep outcomes compared with any control in adults with insomnia.
FINDINGS: DHIs significantly improved insomnia severity (SMD −0.91, 95% CI −1.12 to −0.70), sleep efficiency (SMD 0.59, 95% CI 0.45–0.72), total sleep time (SMD 0.20, 95% CI 0.11–0.29), and sleep quality (SMD −0.61, 95% CI −0.78 to −0.45). However, 95% prediction intervals crossed the null for insomnia severity (−2.04 to 0.22), total sleep time (−0.05 to 0.46), and all secondary outcomes. GRADE certainty ranged from very low to moderate.
INTERPRETATION: The pooled effects are statistically significant but heterogeneous and context-dependent, with wide prediction intervals and low-to-moderate certainty. Subgroup analyses suggest larger benefits in high-income settings and with specific modalities, indicating that DHI efficacy is not uniform. The clinical importance of the average effects is uncertain given prediction intervals crossing the null and effect sizes that may fall below minimum clinically important differences.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: DHIs should not replace face-to-face CBT-I but may serve as low-intensity, adjunctive options in stepped-care models. Clinicians should consider local resources, patient preferences, and implementation context when recommending DHIs, and monitor outcomes to guide ongoing treatment decisions.

item.title: [10] Guided self-help for depression adapted for autistic adults: a multi-centre randomised controlled phase 3 trial (ADEPT-2).
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Autistic adults experience high rates of depression but may not benefit optimally from standard first-line treatments like Guided Self-Help (GSH). This multi-centre phase 3 RCT (ADEPT-2) tested whether autism-adapted GSH (AASH-DEP) improves depressive symptoms versus treatment as usual (TAU) in autistic adults with moderate depression.
FINDINGS: 266 adults (mean age ~35 years, 53% female) were randomised to AASH-DEP (n=132) or TAU (n=134). At 16 weeks, the adjusted mean BDI-II reduction favoured AASH-DEP by 5.05 points (95% CI: -7.85 to -2.24; p<0.001; Cohen’s d=0.47). 81% of AASH-DEP participants completed ≥6 sessions; effects persisted at 52 weeks. No serious adverse events were reported.
INTERPRETATION: The trial shows a moderate, statistically significant advantage of autism-adapted GSH over TAU at 16 weeks, maintained at one year. Strengths include a robust RCT design, clear intervention fidelity, and intention-to-treat analysis. Limitations include reliance on self-report (BDI-II), lack of assessor blinding, and potential selection bias (community-recruited, higher-functioning sample). The effect size (d=0.47) is modest and may not translate to large clinical change for all patients.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: AASH-DEP appears a viable adapted first-line option for autistic adults with moderate depression, particularly where standard GSH is ineffective or poorly tolerated. Clinicians should consider offering autism-specific adaptations and monitor for engagement and tolerability.

item.title: [10] An animated online module for opioid use disorder training in medical students: a sequential mixed-methods evaluation.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This sequential mixed-methods study evaluated a brief animated online module on opioid use disorder (OUD) training among final-year medical students in Saudi Arabia, addressing gaps in communication, stigma reduction, and empathic interviewing skills. The study compared pre/post changes in self-assessed competencies between students receiving a standard lecture alone versus those receiving the lecture followed by the animated module.
FINDINGS: A total of 278 students participated (201 in the lecture → module cohort, 77 in the lecture-only cohort). Both cohorts showed improvements across six domains, but no domain demonstrated a greater pre-post gain during the module period compared to the lecture-only period. Statistically smaller gains were observed during the module period for consequences/risks of OUD, DSM-5 diagnostic approach, and harm reduction, while no significant differences were found for methadone knowledge, buprenorphine knowledge, or empathic stance. Post-module acceptability ratings were high (mean ~4/5 across organization, engagement, relevance, and satisfaction).
INTERPRETATION: The study design (non-randomized, sequential cohorts with non-equivalent baseline timing) limits causal inference about the module’s incremental effect. The lack of detectable superiority over lecture-only training suggests the module did not enhance learning beyond standard didactics in this context. Qualitative feedback highlighted perceived value for engagement and communication, but these findings cannot be attributed to the module alone. The study underscores the need for randomized or counterbalanced trials with aligned baselines and objective outcomes to assess true effectiveness.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The animated module may serve as a feasible and acceptable supplementary tool for OUD training, particularly for fostering engagement and empathic communication, but current evidence does not support its superiority over traditional lectures for improving knowledge or skills. Further rigorous evaluation is required before recommending routine adoption.

item.title: [10] Efficacy and Safety of Intensive Continuous Theta Burst Stimulation Over the Right Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex in Insomnia Disorder:A Randomized Sham-Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This randomized sham-controlled trial (n=30) tested whether 10 days of continuous theta burst stimulation (cTBS) over the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex improves insomnia symptoms and quality of life in adults with DSM-5 insomnia disorder (SCI <16).
FINDINGS: Both active and sham groups improved significantly on all outcomes (all within-group P<.001; large effect sizes). Group×time interactions were nonsignificant for sleep-specific measures (PSQI: F=3.32, P=.060; SCI: F=2.14, P=.147; ISI: F=0.23, P=.720; FOSQ-10: F=0.88, P=.388). A significant interaction favoring active cTBS was found for WHOQOL-BREF (F=8.92, P=.002, ηp²=0.242). Three participants reported transient mild headache; no serious adverse events occurred.
INTERPRETATION: The study is small (n=30), underpowered for sleep endpoints, and shows no significant benefit of active cTBS over sham on insomnia severity or sleep quality. The observed advantage in health-related quality of life is statistically significant but based on a single secondary outcome with a modest effect size (ηp²=0.242). The lack of objective sleep measures (e.g., polysomnography) and short follow-up (2 weeks) limit conclusions. The absence of serious adverse events supports safety, but efficacy for core insomnia symptoms remains unproven.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support routine use of right DLPFC-targeted cTBS for insomnia disorder. Larger trials with objective sleep endpoints and longer follow-up are needed before considering this intervention in practice.

item.title: [10] Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Pharmacovigilance for Neuropsychiatric Therapies: Advancing U.S. Drug Safety Surveillance and Regulatory Decision-Making.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review evaluates the limitations of current U.S. post-marketing drug safety surveillance systems for neuropsychiatric medications and explores how artificial intelligence (AI) could enhance pharmacovigilance. It synthesizes literature since 2000 on adverse event detection, regulatory systems (FAERS, MedWatch, Sentinel, REMS), and AI applications in psychiatric adverse event monitoring.
FINDINGS: Spontaneous reporting systems miss most adverse drug reactions, particularly psychiatric effects, due to underreporting, stigma, and diagnostic challenges. Disproportionality signals (e.g., dissociation and suicidal ideation with esketamine) may be inflated by notoriety bias or confounding by indication. AI tools like natural language processing (NLP) can extract adverse events from free-text psychiatric records with good accuracy, and large language models (LLMs) show early promise in structuring adverse event narratives. However, most AI studies are retrospective proofs of concept, and models trained on biased data risk reproducing inequities.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and heterogeneous, relying on narrative synthesis rather than quantitative meta-analysis. Strengths include a broad review of regulatory systems and AI applications, but limitations include the lack of prospective validation, potential biases in AI training data, and the absence of effect sizes or confidence intervals. The clinical significance of AI tools remains uncertain until they are tested in live pharmacovigilance workflows and linked with electronic health records or claims data.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current AI tools are not yet ready for routine use in psychiatric pharmacovigilance but may help prioritize signal detection in the future. Clinicians should remain vigilant for underreported psychiatric adverse effects and advocate for improved reporting systems and reduced stigma.

item.title: [9] Therapist-supported versus self-guided digital CBT for chronic pain with neurodevelopmental traits: A pilot feasibility randomized controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This three-arm pilot randomized controlled trial (RCT) tested the feasibility of a brief digital CBT program tailored for adults with chronic pain and comorbid neurodevelopmental traits (ASD/ADHD). It compared therapist-supported versus self-guided digital CBT against a sham control to assess acceptability, safety, and preliminary efficacy on pain catastrophizing and depressive symptoms.
FINDINGS: Of 44 randomized adults, 90.9% (40/44) completed post-intervention assessments, and 93.5% (29/31) of those assigned to CBT completed the program, with all rating it as safe. Both self-guided and therapist-supported CBT groups showed significantly greater reductions in pain catastrophizing versus sham (p = .006 and p = .035, respectively), with no clear difference between CBT formats. Depressive symptoms followed a similar pattern. Other outcomes did not differ significantly.
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates strong feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary signals of efficacy, but it is underpowered for definitive between-group comparisons. The lack of blinding in the sham condition and the reliance on self-reported NDD diagnoses are key limitations. The observed effects, while statistically significant, are preliminary and require confirmation in a larger, adequately powered RCT with longer follow-up and systematic monitoring of adverse effects.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest that brief digital CBT tailored for chronic pain with NDD traits is feasible and potentially beneficial, but current evidence is insufficient to recommend one format over the other or to change standard practice. Further research is needed before clinical implementation.

item.title: [9] Clinical and Economic Burdens of ADHD Across Developmental Stages: A Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review synthesizes evidence on the clinical and economic burdens of ADHD across the lifespan, including direct medical costs, non-medical costs, and family-related impacts. It prioritizes large population-based studies, administrative claims data, longitudinal investigations, and meta-analyses published between 2000 and 2026.
FINDINGS: ADHD is consistently associated with substantial healthcare costs (e.g., diagnostic assessment, treatment, and management of comorbidities), non-medical costs (educational support, occupational losses, accidents, and criminal justice involvement), and significant family burdens (reduced productivity, increased caregiving demands, and elevated risks of depression, anxiety, and stress among caregivers). While specific cost figures vary by region and study design, the overall economic impact is consistently high across developmental stages.
INTERPRETATION: The strength of this review lies in its comprehensive synthesis of diverse evidence types, including large-scale administrative and longitudinal studies, which enhances the reliability of its conclusions. However, as a narrative review, it is subject to selection bias and does not provide pooled quantitative estimates (e.g., effect sizes or confidence intervals). The heterogeneity in cost estimation methods and regional differences limits direct comparability. The clinical implications are plausible but require cautious interpretation, as the review does not establish causality or quantify the magnitude of burden reduction achievable through specific interventions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should consider assessing functional and family-level burdens alongside core ADHD symptoms, screen for comorbidities, and ensure continuity of care during transitions (e.g., to adult services). While the review supports integrated, holistic care, it does not provide actionable thresholds or cost-effectiveness data to guide specific treatment choices.

item.title: [6] 2-AG as a potential biomarker for predicting response to short-term fluoxetine treatment in a mouse model of depression.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This preclinical study in male mice exposed to chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) examined whether hippocampal and prefrontal cortical metabolomic changes—specifically endocannabinoid and neurotransmitter levels—could predict early antidepressant response to short-term fluoxetine treatment.
FINDINGS: Behavioral improvement after one week of fluoxetine was associated with a significant increase in hippocampal 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) levels (exact magnitude not reported). In the prefrontal cortex, fluoxetine was linked to reduced GABA and glutamate levels (no numerical values provided). The study used liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry to quantify metabolites in brain tissue.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and limited to a mouse model, so translation to humans is uncertain. The lack of effect sizes, confidence intervals, and p-values in the abstract makes it difficult to assess statistical robustness. While the findings suggest a potential role for 2-AG as a biomarker, the study’s internal validity is constrained by its animal design, absence of human validation, and unclear analytical rigor (e.g., multiple comparisons not addressed). External validity is limited by the use of male mice only and a specific stress protocol.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, this study does not change clinical practice. It highlights a potential research direction—endocannabinoid system modulation in antidepressant response—but requires replication in human studies with rigorous methodology before any biomarker application can be considered.

item.title: [6] Conceptualization and Management of Suicide Risk in Individuals with a History of Traumatic Brain Injury.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines suicide risk in individuals with a history of traumatic brain injury (TBI), focusing on clinical management and the paucity of targeted intervention research. It synthesizes current recommendations for screening, risk assessment, and intervention strategies tailored to TBI sequelae.
FINDINGS: The review highlights that TBI is linked to elevated suicide risk, functional impairment, and psychiatric symptoms, necessitating routine suicide prevention within TBI care. Screening tools and risk management strategies are suggested to incorporate TBI-specific adaptations, such as direct language and visual aids. However, the evidence base for suicide interventions in TBI is limited, with few targeted trials and small, non-generalizable samples.
INTERPRETATION: The strength of this review lies in its practical guidance for clinicians managing suicide risk in TBI patients, emphasizing tailored approaches. However, as a narrative review, it lacks the methodological rigor of a systematic review or meta-analysis, and its recommendations are not evidence-based. The lack of high-quality trials underscores a critical gap in the literature, making it unclear which interventions are most effective for this population.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should remain vigilant for suicide risk in TBI patients and consider adapted screening and management strategies. However, the absence of robust intervention trials means that current practices are largely based on expert opinion rather than empirical evidence. Further research is urgently needed to guide evidence-based suicide prevention in TBI.

item.title: [20] Efficacy and safety of theta-burst stimulation for obsessive-compulsive disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy and safety of theta-burst stimulation (TBS) as an adjunctive treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) by synthesizing data from randomized clinical trials (RCTs). The clinical question was whether TBS reduces OCD symptoms (measured by Y-BOCS) and depressive symptoms (measured by HAM-D) compared to sham stimulation.
FINDINGS: Eight RCTs and one open-label study (n=305) were included. Immediate effects of TBS showed a modest but significant improvement only in the obsession subscale (MD = -1.04, 95% CI [-1.87, -0.22], p=0.01, I²=0%). Long-term effects showed significant improvements in both obsession (MD = -1.63, 95% CI [-2.81, -0.44], p=0.007, I²=31%) and compulsion subscales (MD = -1.68, 95% CI [-2.57, -0.8], p=0.0002, I²=0%), as well as depressive symptoms (MD = -2.16, 95% CI [-3.89, -0.43], p=0.01, I²=15%).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests that TBS may provide small but statistically significant benefits for OCD symptoms, particularly in the long term, with low heterogeneity across studies. However, the clinical significance of these effects is uncertain given the small effect sizes (Y-BOCS reductions of ~1.6 points on subscales). The included studies were RCTs, but the open-label study introduces potential bias. The review did not report adverse effects in detail, though it concluded that TBS was well-tolerated. More high-quality, longer-term RCTs with larger sample sizes are needed to confirm efficacy and assess durability of effects.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: TBS may be considered as an adjunctive treatment for OCD, particularly for patients with prominent obsessional symptoms or comorbid depression, but the modest effect sizes suggest limited clinical impact. Clinicians should weigh these modest benefits against the lack of established long-term efficacy and potential resource requirements for TBS administration.

item.title: [10] From preconception risk to perinatal outcomes: machine learning prediction of depression and acute psychiatric care from electronic health records in the UK.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether routinely collected preconception electronic health record (EHR) data could predict perinatal depressive episodes and the need for acute psychiatric admission or home treatment among 20,793 pregnancies in 14,134 women already receiving secondary mental healthcare in the UK (2012–2020). The clinical question was whether early risk stratification is feasible to guide perinatal mental health care.
FINDINGS: About 16% of pregnancies were associated with a perinatal depressive episode, with 19% of these involving acute psychiatric admission or home treatment. Models predicting depressive episodes showed moderate discrimination (AUC 0.67–0.68), with sensitivity 61–63% and specificity 72–75%. Key predictors included preconception depressive and positive symptom severity, prior psychotropic use (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilisers), primiparity, and socioeconomic deprivation. Smoking during pregnancy was linked to postnatal depression. Models predicting acute psychiatric admission/home treatment had lower discrimination (AUC 0.63), sensitivity 42%, and specificity 84–85%, with predictors including prior antipsychotic/hypnotic use and Black ethnicity.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests that preconception EHR data can moderately predict perinatal depression risk, which may help target monitoring and preventive care. However, prediction of acute psychiatric deterioration remains limited in accuracy. The retrospective design, lack of external validation, and reliance on secondary care populations limit generalisability. The moderate AUC values indicate statistical but not strong clinical discrimination, and the model may not yet be ready for routine use without further validation and integration of longitudinal data.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings support the use of preconception clinical data to flag women at higher risk of perinatal depression for closer follow-up, but prediction of acute deterioration remains insufficiently reliable. Clinicians should be cautious about over-reliance on these models until validated in broader settings and with additional data sources.

item.title: [10] The Hope Paradox: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Association Between Hope and the Acquired Capability to Enact Suicide.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether Snyder’s hope theory (pathways and agency) is paradoxically associated with higher acquired capability for suicide, a construct linked to reduced fear of death and increased pain tolerance. Nine cross-sectional samples (N = 1 896) were synthesized to quantify the association and explore moderators.
FINDINGS: Total hope showed a small but significant positive correlation with acquired capability (r = 0.23, p < 0.001). Both pathways (r = 0.22, p < 0.001) and agency (r = 0.16, p < 0.001) were similarly associated. Heterogeneity was notable for agency, and meta-regression indicated that older age strengthened the association (p = 0.003).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is small, cross-sectional, and heterogeneous, limiting causal inference. The pooled effects are statistically significant yet modest in magnitude, suggesting only a weak link between hope and suicide capability. The stronger association in older adults may reflect cohort or measurement differences rather than a robust clinical phenomenon. High risk of confounding and selection bias weakens internal validity; external validity is uncertain given the predominance of non-clinical or mixed samples.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not justify altering risk assessment or treatment based solely on hope levels. Clinicians should remain cautious about assuming that fostering hope is universally protective; integrating reasons-for-living and adaptive goal-setting may be prudent until longitudinal data clarify the paradox.

item.title: [9] ACOEM Guidelines: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS).
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The ACOEM guideline provides evidence-based recommendations for diagnosing and treating Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS), a chronic pain condition, based on a systematic literature review of diagnostic and treatment methods.
FINDINGS: The guideline recommends first-line treatments including education, strengthening/aerobic exercise, fear avoidance training, NSAIDs, oral glucocorticosteroids, and bisphosphonates. Second-line options include mirror therapy, pain exposure therapy, virtual reality, desensitization, antidepressants (TCAs/SNRIs), gabapentin, and DMSO. Third-line treatments are stellate ganglion and bretylium blocks, with spinal cord stimulator (SCS) implantation as a fourth-line option.
INTERPRETATION: As a guideline, this work synthesizes existing evidence but does not present original data; its strength depends on the quality of underlying studies. The recommendations are structured by treatment tiers, but the evidence base may vary in robustness across interventions. The clinical applicability hinges on the availability of multidisciplinary resources (e.g., VR, pain exposure therapy) and patient tolerance for invasive procedures.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians may use this framework to guide CRPS management, prioritizing non-invasive therapies first. However, the guideline does not quantify effect sizes or compare treatments directly, so individual patient preferences and local resource constraints remain critical in decision-making.

item.title: [28] Comparative efficacy and tolerability of pharmacological interventions for the acute treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder across the lifespan: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and network meta-analysis compared the short-term efficacy and tolerability of pharmacological treatments for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) across the lifespan, synthesizing double-blind RCTs with 8–16 week outcomes.
FINDINGS: 52 RCTs (n=7316) were included: 9 in children/adolescents (n=822) and 43 in adults (n=6494). In youth, clomipramine showed the largest efficacy vs placebo (SMD −1.19, 95% CI −1.73 to −0.64) and superiority over several SSRIs (e.g., vs fluoxetine SMD −0.75, −1.39 to −0.11). In adults, clomipramine (SMD −0.71, −0.88 to −0.54) and several SSRIs (e.g., fluvoxamine SMD −0.63, −0.83 to −0.43) outperformed placebo; clomipramine was more efficacious than fluoxetine (SMD −0.34, −0.65 to −0.04). Tolerability was lower for clomipramine (OR 4.65 vs placebo, 3.27–6.60) and several SSRIs; clomipramine was less tolerable than most active comparators.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests clomipramine has the greatest efficacy but poorer tolerability than SSRIs, with stronger comparative signals in children/adolescents. CINeMA ratings ranged from low to high, and heterogeneity in included populations and limited ethnicity reporting temper confidence. The trade-off between efficacy and adverse effects should guide individualized decisions rather than blanket recommendations.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clomipramine remains a first-line option for severe OCD when efficacy is paramount, but clinicians should anticipate higher discontinuation due to adverse events and discuss this trade-off with patients. SSRIs remain reasonable alternatives with better tolerability profiles.

item.title: [26] The impact of cognitive behavioral therapy and third-wave therapies on the quality of life of patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 RCTs (n=1,324) assessed whether cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and third-wave therapies improve quality of life in adults with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).
FINDINGS: The pooled standardised mean difference (SMD) for quality of life favoured CBT/third-wave therapies versus control (SMD 0.18, 95 % CI 0.06–0.29, P = 0.004). Heterogeneity was zero (I² = 0 %), sensitivity analyses were stable, and publication bias was low. Subgroup effects were generally non-significant except for non-European settings and short-term interventions.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate-sized, low in heterogeneity, and at low risk of bias, supporting a modest but statistically significant benefit on quality of life. The small effect size (SMD ≈ 0.18) suggests limited clinical impact for individual patients, and subgroup findings are exploratory and not definitive. Longer-term, multi-centre RCTs with active comparators and validated QoL instruments are needed to confirm durability and generalisability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current data imply that offering CBT or third-wave therapies may yield a small improvement in OCD patients’ quality of life, but expectations should be modest; routine practice need not change until larger confirmatory trials are published.

item.title: [20] Digital Health Interventions for Pregnancy- and Childbirth-Related Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Symptoms in Postpartum Women: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated whether digital health interventions reduce pregnancy- or childbirth-related posttraumatic stress disorder (PCR-PTSD) symptoms in postpartum women, with secondary outcomes on depression and anxiety. Ten randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 1,026 participants were identified.
FINDINGS: Immediately post-intervention, digital interventions showed a moderate reduction in PTSD symptoms (SMD −0.59, 95% CI −0.98 to −0.19; P=.01), but with substantial heterogeneity (I²=79.86%). The pooled effect at longest follow-up was not statistically significant (SMD −0.36, 95% CI −1.00 to 0.27; P=.20). Prediction intervals crossed the null in all analyses. Subgroup differences by provider involvement were noted but exploratory.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests short-term benefits of digital interventions for PCR-PTSD, but confidence is limited by high heterogeneity, wide prediction intervals, and lack of sustained effects at follow-up. The findings are preliminary and should be interpreted cautiously due to risk of bias in included trials and unclear clinical significance of the effect size.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Digital interventions may offer a short-term adjunct for PCR-PTSD, but current evidence does not support sustained benefit or clear clinical impact. Further high-quality RCTs with longer follow-up and clinically meaningful outcomes are needed before recommending routine use.

item.title: [19] Perioperative esketamine and postoperative sleep quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluated whether perioperative esketamine improves postoperative sleep quality in surgical patients, a clinically relevant issue given the high prevalence of postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) and its impact on recovery.
FINDINGS: Twenty-three RCTs (n=2868) showed esketamine improved sleep quality on postoperative days (POD) 1 (ROM 0.85, 95% CI 0.80–0.90), POD 2 (ROM 0.73, 95% CI 0.57–0.93), POD 3 (ROM 0.94, 95% CI 0.90–0.99), and POD 7 (ROM 0.89, 95% CI 0.82–0.95). Incidence of PSD was reduced on PODs 1–3 (RRs 0.71, 0.70, 0.61; all P ≤ 0.01), with no benefit at 1 month. Esketamine also lowered postoperative pain and depression scores but increased drowsiness (RR 12.64, 95% CI 6.04–26.46).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests short-term benefits of esketamine on sleep and related outcomes, but heterogeneity (I² up to 92%) and lack of long-term data limit certainty. The large effect on drowsiness is clinically important and may offset benefits. The review is well-conducted but relies on small, single-center trials with variable dosing and outcomes, reducing generalizability to routine perioperative care.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support routine use of perioperative esketamine for sleep improvement; benefits are modest and short-lived, with a notable risk of sedation. Further large, high-quality RCTs are needed before considering clinical implementation.

item.title: [17] The efficacy and safety of olanzapine combined with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) in patients with comorbid anxiety-depression and sleep disorders.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This retrospective non-randomized cohort study assessed whether adding repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) to olanzapine improves sleep, anxiety, and depression in adults with comorbid anxiety-depression and sleep disorders over 4 weeks.
FINDINGS: 210 patients were allocated to olanzapine monotherapy (n=102) or olanzapine plus rTMS (n=108). Actigraphy showed higher sleep efficiency (80.31% vs 76.85%), longer total sleep time (404.26 vs 398.26 minutes), and fewer nighttime awakenings (3.78 vs 4.12) with combined therapy. Sleep scales improved more with rTMS (PSQI 8.49 vs 9.05; ISI 11.47 vs 11.91). Mood/anxiety scales also improved more with combined therapy (HAM-D 13.51 vs 14.12; HAM-A 12.61 vs 13.37). Adverse events were mostly mild; headache was more frequent with rTMS.
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests short-term benefits of olanzapine plus rTMS on sleep and mood, but the retrospective non-randomized design, lack of blinding, and 4-week follow-up limit internal validity. Residual confounding cannot be excluded, and metabolic outcomes did not differ. Confirmation in randomized, longer-term trials is needed to assess durability and safety.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence supports short-term adjunctive rTMS for sleep and mood symptoms in this population, but routine adoption should await confirmatory trials due to design limitations. Monitor for headache and metabolic effects.

item.title: [15] A successful clozapine rechallenge in a patient with treatment-resistant schizophrenia:A case report.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This single case report asks whether clozapine can be safely reintroduced after neutropenia in a patient with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, and whether lithium co-therapy can mitigate hematologic risk. The study design is a case report of a 31-year-old woman with a 16-year history of schizophrenia.
FINDINGS: Clozapine was discontinued at 300 mg/day when neutropenia (ANC 1,414/μL) occurred during a viral-like illness. After relapse on alternative antipsychotics, clozapine was restarted with lithium. Hematologic parameters remained stable, psychotic symptoms improved markedly, and clozapine was titrated to 450 mg/day with lithium 800 mg/day. A single generalized tonic-clonic seizure occurred at these doses; dose reduction restored stability without further seizures.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is anecdotal (n=1) and subject to multiple confounders (viral illness, dose titration, seizure threshold). No control, blinding, or statistical analysis is possible. The authors attribute stability to revised Japanese monitoring guidelines and lithium’s granulocyte-stimulating effect, but causality cannot be inferred. The seizure at higher doses underscores the narrow therapeutic window in rechallenge scenarios.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This report suggests that, under strict hematologic monitoring and with lithium co-therapy, cautious clozapine rechallenge may be feasible after neutropenia; however, it does not establish safety or efficacy and should not change routine practice beyond individualized, multidisciplinary decision-making.

item.title: [15] Exploring the Association Between Cannabis Use and Male Reproductive Parameters: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether cannabis use is associated with male reproductive parameters (sperm quality and serum hormones) in men, addressing a gap in fertility assessment guidelines. Eighteen studies (5,766 participants) were pooled for sperm outcomes and 21,066 participants for hormonal outcomes, all reporting cannabis users smoked ≥1 joint/week.
FINDINGS: Cannabis users had significantly lower sperm morphology scores than non-users (MD = -1.02; 95% CI: -1.93 to -0.10; p < 0.05), with the effect persisting in WHO-criteria–restricted analyses. No significant differences were found for sperm concentration, motility, volume, or total count. Hormonally, only SHBG was elevated in users (MD = 3.90; 95% CI: 1.67–6.13; p < 0.05), while testosterone, FSH, and LH showed no differences.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate-sized but heterogeneous (I² not reported), and all studies relied on self-reported cannabis exposure, raising misclassification risk. The observed effect on morphology is statistically significant but small in magnitude and of uncertain clinical relevance for fertility outcomes. The lack of association with other semen parameters and most hormones tempers concern, though residual confounding (e.g., tobacco co-use) cannot be excluded. Causality remains unproven.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Cannabis use may warrant inclusion in preconception counseling for men with unexplained infertility or abnormal sperm morphology, but current findings do not mandate routine abstinence or specific fertility interventions. Further high-quality studies with objective cannabis exposure measures and fertility endpoints are needed.

item.title: [11] Rethinking University Mental Health for the AI Era: From Crisis Response to Core Mission.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This perspective piece synthesizes epidemiologic and clinical trial data to argue for a university-wide, stepped-care model integrating digital tools and regulated AI to address the rising mental health crisis among college students. It draws on large-scale surveys (WMH-ICS), RCTs of digital interventions, and implementation studies to propose a scalable, governance-anchored system.
FINDINGS: WMH-ICS data indicate 37–58 % of first-year students meet 12-month DSM-5 criteria for a mental disorder, yet treatment rates are low and academic impairment is substantial. Hybrid stepped-care models—combining universal prevention, guided digital interventions, and task-sharing roles such as digital navigators—are highlighted as scalable solutions that preserve clinician time and improve access.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative synthesis without formal meta-analysis or quantitative effect sizes, the strength of evidence rests on cited external studies rather than new data. The proposal is conceptually coherent and aligns with emerging digital mental health literature, but lacks direct empirical validation of the proposed integrated model. Key uncertainties include long-term safety, equity impacts, and governance mechanisms for AI within university settings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The paper supports a shift toward prevention-focused, digitally enabled university mental health systems, but clinicians should await empirical evaluation of the proposed model before adopting AI-driven components in routine care.

item.title: [10] Assessing the psychometric properties of the Symptom Checklist Five-Items (SCL-5) instrument in a clinical setting for treating intimate partner violence.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study assessed whether the 5-item Symptom Checklist (SCL-5) is reliable and valid for measuring mental health symptoms in a clinical population of intimate-partner-violence (IPV) perpetrators and their partners, a group with high symptom burden not previously studied with this instrument.
FINDINGS: No floor or ceiling effects were detected (highest floor 8.7 %, ceiling 1.9 %). Internal consistency was high (Cronbach’s α = 0.86 overall; 0.83 perpetrators, 0.89 partners). Area under the ROC curve for detecting clinically significant distress was 94.6 % overall (95 % CI 0.913–0.978), 93.5 % for perpetrators and 96.9 % for partners. Over one year, mean SCL-5 scores fell from 1.98 to 1.74 (mean change −0.24, 95 % CI −0.36 to −0.12; t = −4.021, p < 0.001), with 54 % of participants showing a decrease.
INTERPRETATION: The COSMIN-guided validation provides strong internal-validity evidence for SCL-5 in this IPV sample. Responsiveness was demonstrated by a statistically significant decline in scores over one year, though the effect size (Cohen’s d ≈ 0.3) is modest. The sample is modest (N = 161) and limited to one Norwegian clinic, so generalisability to other settings or languages remains uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: SCL-5 appears suitable for routine symptom monitoring in IPV treatment programs, but clinicians should not equate a statistically significant change with a large clinical improvement; small average shifts may still be meaningful at the individual level.

item.title: [9] Canadian guidelines for post COVID-19 condition (CAN-PCC): A summary for general practitioners.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The Canadian Guidelines for Post COVID-19 Condition (CAN-PCC) provide evidence-based recommendations for general practitioners (GPs) on the prevention, diagnosis, and management of Long COVID, a condition with significant global burden. Developed by a multidisciplinary team using GRADE methodology, the guidelines synthesize over 100 recommendations across multiple domains.
FINDINGS: Key recommendations include: (1) **Diagnosis**: A conditional recommendation for symptom-guided work-up and a strong recommendation to screen adults for depression. (2) **Clinical interventions**: Conditional recommendations for patient-centered goals, functional recovery, targeted pharmacotherapy, and non-pharmacological strategies. (3) **Prevention**: Conditional recommendations for vaccination, masking, improving indoor air quality, and early outpatient pharmacotherapy (e.g., metformin, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir). (4) **Pediatrics**: Conditional recommendations for vaccination and mental-health screening, with a strong recommendation against cannabidiol (CBD). The guidelines emphasize adaptability across diverse healthcare settings.
INTERPRETATION: The CAN-PCC guidelines are based on a systematic synthesis of evidence using GRADE methodology, which enhances their rigor and transparency. However, many recommendations are conditional (low to moderate certainty evidence), reflecting evolving research and heterogeneity in PCC presentation. The strong recommendation against CBD in pediatrics is notable for its clarity, but other recommendations are less definitive due to limited high-quality evidence. The guidelines provide a practical framework for GPs but should be adapted to local contexts and updated as new evidence emerges.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: GPs should prioritize symptom-guided evaluation, routine depression screening in adults, and functional recovery-focused care for PCC patients. Prevention strategies (vaccination, indoor air quality) and early pharmacotherapy (where indicated) are emphasized, though evidence for these is still developing. Pediatric care should include mental health screening and avoid CBD. Clinicians should remain cautious about overgeneralizing recommendations due to the conditional nature of much of the evidence.

item.title: [9] A call for action: Guidelines for implementation of mental health services at the community level.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Mental health conditions contribute substantially to global disease burden, yet access to care at the community level remains limited. This qualitative study aimed to identify key components for guideline development to implement mental health services within Ward-Based Primary Health Care Outreach Teams (WBPHCOTs) in South Africa.
FINDINGS: Using a Nominal Group Technique with 11 purposively selected experts, the study generated consensus on seven guideline components: household visits, collaboration with key stakeholders, staff training, mental health prevention and promotion, treatment adherence support, professional supervision, and strengthening community services.
INTERPRETATION: This is a small, expert-driven qualitative consensus study with no quantitative outcomes or patient involvement. While it provides structured input for guideline development, the findings are preliminary and not generalizable beyond the local context. The lack of external validation and limited sample size are notable weaknesses. The proposed components align with known community mental health principles but require further evaluation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings may inform local guideline development for community mental health outreach in South Africa, but should not be used to guide practice without broader stakeholder input and empirical testing.

item.title: [8] Clinical Risk Factors for Suicide in Persons With Epilepsy: A Nationwide Population-Based Case-Control Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study investigated clinical risk factors for suicide in persons with epilepsy using a nationwide population-based case-control design in Sweden (2006–2011), addressing an important gap in understanding suicide risk in this vulnerable group.
FINDINGS: The study included 111 suicide cases and 1,147 controls. Key findings showed strong associations with alcohol abuse (OR 11.81, 95% CI 6.25–22.30) and substance abuse (OR 10.71, 95% CI 4.52–25.38), depression (OR 2.94, 95% CI 1.56–5.53), and anxiety disorders (OR 2.93, 95% CI 1.57–5.44). Living alone increased risk (OR 2.59, 95% CI 1.58–4.26), and a dose-response relationship was observed with tonic-clonic seizure frequency (highest risk with 4–10 seizures/year: OR 5.01, 95% CI 2.2–11.3). Antiseizure medication (ASM) treatment was associated with lower suicide risk (monotherapy OR 0.51, polytherapy OR 0.21), while nonadherence increased risk (OR 3.02, 95% CI 1.8–5.1).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is moderate in strength due to the case-control design, modest sample size (111 cases), and reliance on registry data with potential unmeasured confounders. The large effect sizes for substance abuse and seizure frequency are notable, but causality cannot be inferred. The protective association of ASM treatment is intriguing but may reflect confounding by indication (e.g., treated patients may have milder epilepsy). The study’s focus on completed suicide and lack of data on prior suicidal behavior limits generalizability to broader suicide risk assessment.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The findings support targeted suicide risk assessment in epilepsy patients with alcohol/substance abuse, high seizure frequency, or nonadherence to ASM. Routine screening for substance use and optimizing seizure control may be prudent, but these results alone do not justify major changes in clinical practice without further validation.

item.title: [7] [Epilepsy and Alcohol].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines the complex relationship between alcohol consumption and epilepsy, focusing on mechanisms, risk factors, and clinical management. It synthesizes current understanding of how alcohol affects seizure risk, withdrawal phenomena, and differential diagnosis in patients with epilepsy.
FINDINGS: Acute alcohol suppresses CNS activity, while sudden cessation of heavy drinking can trigger rebound neuronal hyperexcitability and withdrawal seizures. Heavy or binge drinking increases seizure risk in people with epilepsy, especially when combined with sleep deprivation, poor medication adherence, dehydration, or metabolic disturbances. Alcohol-related seizures must be distinguished from withdrawal seizures, epilepsy-related seizures, and acute symptomatic seizures due to other causes. Benzodiazepines are recommended for acute management of alcohol withdrawal seizures. Evidence on low-level alcohol consumption and seizure risk remains limited.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this paper provides a broad overview rather than new empirical data. Its strength lies in summarizing mechanisms and clinical distinctions, but it lacks quantitative effect sizes or systematic evidence synthesis. The conclusions are largely consistent with clinical consensus, though the evidence base for low-level drinking remains weak. The review does not address confounding variables comprehensively or provide risk estimates.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should assess alcohol use patterns, timing of seizures relative to drinking, withdrawal symptoms, and adherence to antiseizure medication. Benzodiazepines remain the standard for acute alcohol withdrawal seizures. Counseling should emphasize the potential risks of heavy drinking in epilepsy, while acknowledging uncertainty regarding low-level consumption.

item.title: [7] Intervening on Therapy-Interfering Behavior.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review (part 2 of a 2-part series) addresses therapy-interfering behaviors (TIBs) in psychiatric treatment, aiming to improve patient engagement and reduce suicide risk. It focuses on identifying contexts where TIBs emerge and strategies to address them.
FINDINGS: The article discusses common contexts for TIBs, such as avoidance, non-adherence, or hostility, and suggests exploring their functional purpose (e.g., emotion regulation, escape from distress). It proposes methods like motivational interviewing, contingency management, and dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) techniques to address these behaviors. However, no quantitative data (e.g., effect sizes, p-values) or empirical study results are provided.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review without original data or systematic methodology, the strength of evidence is low. The recommendations are based on clinical experience and theoretical frameworks rather than empirical testing. The lack of quantitative outcomes limits conclusions about effectiveness or generalizability. The discussion may be useful for conceptual understanding but cannot guide practice changes without further evidence.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This article highlights the importance of addressing TIBs in psychiatric care but does not provide actionable, evidence-based strategies. Clinicians may find the conceptual framework helpful for reflection but should await empirical validation before adopting the proposed methods.

item.title: [6] The Complex Relationship Between ADHD and Alcohol Use Disorder: A Narrative Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines the comorbidity between ADHD and alcohol use disorder (AUD), focusing on mechanisms, diagnostic challenges, and treatment strategies. It synthesizes epidemiological, neurobiological, and psychosocial evidence to address a clinically significant issue in dual-diagnosis care.
FINDINGS: ADHD is associated with earlier alcohol initiation, more severe drinking patterns, and poorer treatment outcomes in AUD. Impulsivity, executive dysfunction, and dopaminergic dysregulation are implicated in increased susceptibility to alcohol dependence. Diagnostic overlap—such as cognitive impairments and alcohol withdrawal mimicking ADHD symptoms—complicates assessment. While stimulants may improve impulse control and executive function, their role in preventing alcohol misuse remains uncertain. Nonstimulant medications (e.g., atomoxetine, guanfacine) and anti-craving agents (e.g., naltrexone) are discussed as alternatives. Behavioral interventions such as CBT, mindfulness, and motivational enhancement therapy show promise.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this study synthesizes existing literature without new empirical data, limiting causal inference and quantitative effect estimates. The evidence base relies on observational and mechanistic studies, which are prone to confounding and selection bias. The review highlights plausible mechanisms but does not provide pooled effect sizes or head-to-head treatment comparisons. Long-term data on ADHD treatment in AUD populations are notably sparse, and treatment recommendations remain tentative. The discussion of diagnostic challenges is clinically relevant but underscores the need for validated tools in this population.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for ADHD in patients with AUD, especially those with early-onset drinking or persistent impulsivity. While stimulants may help ADHD symptoms, their impact on alcohol outcomes is unclear—close monitoring for misuse is essential. Integrated care combining ADHD management with AUD-specific treatments (e.g., naltrexone, CBT) is advised, but individualized approaches are necessary due to limited high-quality evidence. Routine screening for ADHD in addiction settings may improve outcomes, pending stronger longitudinal data.

item.title: [6] Suicide Risk Screening Among Trans Women: Screening Performance of a Single-Item Self-Report Measure Compared With Clinician-Administered Interview.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study evaluated whether the single-item suicidal ideation question from the PHQ-9 (item 9) accurately identifies suicide risk in trans women, compared with the gold-standard C-SSRS interview. This is clinically important because trans women have high suicide risk and busy psychiatric settings need efficient screening tools.
FINDINGS: Among 79 trans women, PHQ-9 item 9 (≥1) showed strong correlation with passive ideation (rφ=0.79, P<0.001) and nonspecific active ideation (rφ=0.59, P<0.001), but not with other ideation or behavior items. Sensitivity was 43.3% [95% CI: 24.5%, 62.2%], specificity 95.9% [90.2%, 100.0%], positive predictive value 86.7% [67.2%, 100.0%], and negative predictive value 73.4% [62.3%, 84.6%] against the C-SSRS screener.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests the PHQ-9 item 9 has high specificity but low sensitivity for detecting suicide risk in trans women, missing over half of those at risk. The small sample size and single-site design limit generalizability. The study highlights a potential risk of under-detection using this brief tool in a high-risk population.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: PHQ-9 item 9 alone is insufficient for suicide risk screening in trans women; clinicians should use more comprehensive assessments (e.g., full C-SSRS or structured interviews) to avoid missing at-risk patients.

item.title: [30] Comparative efficacy and acceptability of antidepressants in the long-term treatment of major depressive disorder: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and network meta-analysis compared the long-term (>12 weeks) efficacy (sustained response) and acceptability (all-cause discontinuation) of 21 antidepressants in adults with unipolar major depressive disorder using double-blind RCTs. The study aimed to inform treatment choices by synthesizing head-to-head and placebo-controlled trials.
FINDINGS: From 54,231 records, 115 studies (30,428 participants; mean age 45.3 years, 66% female) were included. In 35 head-to-head continuation/continuation-extension trials (n=9,888), escitalopram (OR 1.62, 95% CI 1.21–2.18), duloxetine (OR 1.57, 1.08–2.26), and agomelatine (OR 1.40, 1.06–1.85) showed higher sustained response rates than fluoxetine. Escitalopram (OR 0.60, 0.43–0.83) and duloxetine (OR 0.64, 0.44–0.95) had lower all-cause discontinuation vs. fluoxetine. Bupropion and reboxetine showed lower sustained response, while reboxetine and milnacipran had higher discontinuation rates in pairwise comparisons. Sensitivity analyses including enrichment designs supported these findings, but 54% of trials had high risk of bias.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests modest differences between antidepressants in sustained response and acceptability, with escitalopram and duloxetine appearing favorable. However, high risk of bias in many trials and indirect comparisons limit certainty. The lack of patient involvement and missing demographic data further constrain generalizability. More high-quality, head-to-head RCTs are needed to confirm these findings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These results may guide antidepressant selection for long-term maintenance, favoring escitalopram or duloxetine over fluoxetine in some cases. Clinicians should weigh modest effect sizes against individual patient profiles and monitor tolerability closely.

item.title: [21] Prevalence and outcomes of co-occurring mental/physical comorbidities and substance use disorders: An atlas umbrella review including 156 systematic reviews with meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This umbrella review synthesised 156 systematic reviews with meta-analyses to map the prevalence and outcomes of co-occurring substance use disorders (SUDs) with psychiatric and somatic conditions, aiming to inform screening and care strategies.
FINDINGS: High-credibility estimates showed ADHD with a pooled SUD prevalence of 21.0% (95% CI 17.0–25.0; k = 31) and major depressive disorder with 36.1% (95% CI 32.4–39.7; k = 161) among patients with opioid use disorder. Chronic opioid analgesic use reached 27.0% (95% CI 23.0–31.0; N > 3.9 M) in non-cancer pain and 40.0% (95% CI 32.0–49.0) after lumbar fusion. Hepatitis C prevalence was 61.0% (95% CI 56.0–67.0) among injection drug users. Syndromal schizotypy correlated strongly with cannabis use disorder (I² = 0%).
INTERPRETATION: The review’s strength lies in its broad scope and credibility grading, but overlap across reviews and reliance on observational data limit causal inference. The reported prevalences are clinically striking and support routine cross-domain screening, yet the review does not evaluate whether such screening improves outcomes. Effect sizes are large but observational, so implementation should proceed alongside trials assessing impact on patient-important endpoints.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should consider routine screening for SUDs across psychiatric and somatic domains, especially in high-prevalence groups such as chronic pain patients on opioids and people who inject drugs, while awaiting evidence that screening changes long-term outcomes.

item.title: [15] Mental Health and Behavioral Factors Associated With Suicidal Ideation Among Students in Africa: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined which mental health and behavioral factors are associated with suicidal ideation among students in Africa, pooling data from 49 studies with 138,915 participants to inform prevention strategies in educational settings.
FINDINGS: Depression (OR 3.92, 95 % CI 2.05–7.49), hopelessness (OR 5.20, 95 % CI 1.99–13.60), and cannabis use (OR 1.44, 95 % CI 1.24–1.66) showed the strongest associations with suicidal ideation. Female sex carried a modestly elevated odds (OR 1.25, 95 % CI 1.18–1.33). All pooled estimates exhibited substantial heterogeneity (I² not reported in abstract).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is large but observational, so causality cannot be inferred. Substantial heterogeneity and reliance on self-report measures limit certainty. Effect sizes for substance use and internalizing symptoms are statistically significant yet modest to moderate; hopelessness shows the largest point estimate but with wide confidence intervals, suggesting imprecision. No funding source is stated in the abstract.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine screening for depression, hopelessness, and substance use in African student populations may help identify those at elevated suicide risk. Clinicians should remain cautious about over-interpreting pooled associations until more longitudinal and interventional data are available.

item.title: [14] Dialogical therapy plus treatment as usual versus treatment as usual in adults with distressing and persistent auditory hallucinations in the UK (Talking with Voices-II): a randomised controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The trial tested whether adding Talking with Voices (TwV), a dialogue-based therapy engaging directly with auditory hallucinations, to treatment-as-usual (TAU) improves personal recovery and other outcomes in adults with serious mental health problems and persistent, distressing voice hearing. It was a rater-blinded, parallel-arm RCT across four UK NHS sites (ISRCTN15897915).
FINDINGS: 309 adults were randomised (156 TwV+TAU, 153 TAU). At 8 months, personal recovery (primary outcome) was higher with TwV (adjusted difference 6.97 [95% CI 5.00–8.95]; p<0.0001; SES=0.63). Twelve of fifteen secondary outcomes favoured TwV (SES 0.18–0.86), including voice-related measures and PTSD symptoms; no effects were seen on dissociation or positive self-beliefs. At 14 months, recovery remained higher but smaller (adjusted difference 3.55 [0.96–6.14]; p=0.0073; SES=0.32). Serious adverse events were similar across groups and unrelated to therapy.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests TwV improves personal recovery and several symptom domains with moderate effect sizes at 8 months, attenuating by 14 months. Strengths include rater blinding, multisite design, and lived-experience co-leadership; limitations include reliance on unadjusted secondary analyses and lack of an active comparator. The clinical significance is plausible but should be weighed against implementation feasibility and durability of effect.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: TwV may be a useful adjunct for patients with persistent, distressing voices seeking personal recovery, but services should plan for sustained delivery and monitor long-term outcomes before widespread adoption.

item.title: [9] Is ibogaine treatment durable? 12-month follow-up of magnesium-ibogaine therapy (MISTIC) in special operations veterans with traumatic brain injuries.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This prospective cohort study assessed whether single-dose magnesium-ibogaine therapy produced durable (12-month) improvements in functional disability and psychiatric symptoms among 30 male U.S. Special Operations Veterans with chronic traumatic brain injury (TBI) sequelae including PTSD, depression, and anxiety.
FINDINGS: Of 30 treated participants, 25 completed 12-month follow-up. Linear mixed-effects models showed sustained reductions in disability and symptom measures (all p < 0.001 after multiple-comparison correction) with large effect sizes (Cohen’s d ≥ 2.18 at 12 months). Survival analyses in immediate remitters estimated 84 % sustained PTSD remission, 66 % for depression, and 61 % for anxiety at 12 months; however, most participants used additional psychedelics or other interventions during follow-up.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s naturalistic, single-arm design precludes causal inference; concurrent use of other treatments and lack of blinding/placebo control limit internal validity. The very large effect sizes are impressive but must be viewed cautiously given the small sample, absence of randomization, and potential confounding. External validity is restricted to male combat veterans with chronic TBI in a high-resource setting. Randomized, placebo-controlled trials are needed to isolate ibogaine’s true effect and durability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These preliminary findings suggest potential long-term benefit of ibogaine for TBI-related psychiatric comorbidity, but they do not yet justify changing practice; clinicians should await robust RCT evidence and remain alert to safety and interaction profiles.

item.title: [9] The gut microbiota dietary index reveals a modifiable diet-depression association varying by BMI and possibly linked to inflammation: a hypothesis-generating modified diet for future intervention research.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study (n=28,884 adults) examined whether a diet supportive of gut microbiota (Dietary Index for Gut Microbiota, DI-GM) is associated with depressive symptoms (PHQ-9), exploring potential BMI interactions and inflammatory mediation in a hypothesis-generating framework.
FINDINGS: Participants with depression had lower DI-GM scores than those without. Regression and generalized additive models showed an inverse association between DI-GM and PHQ-9, stronger at higher BMI. Feature importance analysis highlighted fiber, whole grains, refined grains, and fat intake. Exploratory mediation suggested inflammation may partially explain the association, though a high DI-GM diet lacks key depression-related nutrients (vitamin D, omega-3, zinc).
INTERPRETATION: The study is observational and cannot infer causality. The large sample size strengthens precision, but unmeasured confounders (e.g., lifestyle, medication) and cross-sectional design limit internal validity. The BMI interaction and inflammatory signal are intriguing but exploratory. The lack of clinically meaningful nutrient density in high DI-GM diets further complicates interpretation. Findings are preliminary and require prospective and interventional validation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support dietary modification based on DI-GM for depression management. Clinicians should remain cautious about overinterpreting these associations. Future research should test modified gut-microbiota diets with targeted nutrient supplementation in randomized trials before any practice change.

item.title: [6] Long-acting injectable antipsychotics linked to reduced short-term disruptive life event and death.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This retrospective cohort study examined whether long-acting injectable antipsychotics (LAI) reduce all-cause mortality and disruptive life events (DLE) compared with oral antipsychotics in adults recently diagnosed with schizophrenia (SCZ) or bipolar I disorder (BPI). The study used data from Kaiser Permanente Southern California (2007–2019) and followed patients for one year after an initial mental health emergency or inpatient encounter.
FINDINGS: The cohort included 3,667 patients on oral antipsychotics only and 218 on LAIs. Adjusted analyses suggested lower risks in the LAI group for any DLE (risk difference −1.68%, 95% CI −3.44% to 0.08%, p < 0.10) and all-cause mortality (−0.46%, 95% CI −0.98% to 0.06%, p < 0.10). The rarity of outcomes and small LAI sample limited statistical power.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s retrospective design and small LAI group reduce confidence in the findings. While point estimates favor LAIs, wide confidence intervals crossing zero and p-values just above conventional thresholds mean the results are not statistically significant. Larger, prospective studies are needed to confirm any benefit on mortality or disruptive life events.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not yet justify changing practice to prioritize LAIs solely to reduce short-term mortality or disruptive life events. Shared decision-making should weigh LAI benefits against patient preferences and logistical factors.

item.title: [31] Psychological and psychosocial interventions for the treatment of antenatal maternal depression: systematic review and network meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and network meta-analysis compared non-pharmacological interventions for clinically diagnosed antenatal depression, addressing the clinical question of which psychosocial treatments are most effective and acceptable during pregnancy. Ten RCTs (n=1853) were included.
FINDINGS: Cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) showed the largest reduction in depressive symptoms versus treatment-as-usual (TAU) with a standardised mean difference (SMD) of -0.83 (95% CI -1.38 to -0.28). Other interventions had smaller, less certain effects. Acceptability (dropout rates) did not differ meaningfully between interventions. The certainty of evidence across all comparisons was rated as very low.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is small (only 10 trials) and the certainty of evidence is very low, meaning conclusions are tentative. CBT appears promising, but the wide confidence interval and low certainty suggest results should be interpreted cautiously. The lack of difference in acceptability is reassuring. More high-quality, adequately powered RCTs are needed to confirm these findings and improve confidence in the evidence.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings support CBT as a reasonable first-line non-pharmacological option for antenatal depression, consistent with existing guidelines. However, due to very low certainty, clinicians should remain cautious and consider patient preferences and local availability when choosing interventions.

item.title: [15] Acute and long-term effects of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in major depressive episodes: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of randomized sham-controlled trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of randomized sham-controlled trials examined how different repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) dosing parameters (total pulses, pulses/session, sessions, duration) affect acute and long-term outcomes in adults with major depressive episodes (MDE). The goal was to identify dose ranges where clinical benefits plateau.
FINDINGS: Across 108 trials (134 active arms; n = 5,621), significant non-linear associations were found between dosing dimensions and acute efficacy. The highest predicted acute benefits occurred at approximately 30,000–39,000 total pulses, 1,800–2,200 pulses/session, 14–16 sessions, and 2.7–3.1 weeks of treatment, with limited additional benefit beyond these ranges. Follow-up analyses (after >7 days) showed smaller, mostly linear associations, with optimal doses at 26,000–33,000 total pulses, 1,300–1,800 pulses/session, 10–14 sessions, and 2.8–3.3 weeks. Effect sizes were reported as standardized mean differences and risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals, though exact values were not provided in the abstract.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides robust group-level evidence that rTMS efficacy plateaus within moderate dose ranges, suggesting diminishing returns with higher exposures. Strengths include a large sample size, rigorous dose-response modeling, and sensitivity analyses confirming stability. However, the findings are descriptive and do not establish individualized dosing rules. The follow-up data suggest maintenance strategies may be more critical than further dose escalation. Limitations include heterogeneity in trial protocols and reliance on aggregate data rather than patient-level factors.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These results support using moderate rTMS dosing ranges (e.g., ~15 sessions with ~2,000 pulses/session) for acute MDE treatment, with potential adjustments for maintenance. Clinicians should avoid excessive dose escalation without clear benefit, but individualized tailoring remains uncertain pending further research.

item.title: [15] Trainee psychiatrists' views on clozapine prescribing in Ireland.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: A cross-sectional online survey examined trainee psychiatrists' knowledge, confidence, and perceived barriers to clozapine prescribing in Ireland, a setting where clozapine remains underutilised despite its established efficacy for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS).
FINDINGS: Of ~500 trainees invited, 74 responded (14.8%). Most had clinical exposure to clozapine, but <30% reported specific training. Knowledge of clozapine’s indication in TRS was strong, but varied for therapeutic drug monitoring, dosing, and agranulocytosis risk. Confidence was highest in identifying TRS and monitoring mental state, but lower for physical health monitoring, managing adverse effects, discontinuation, and rechallenge. Barriers included adherence concerns, blood monitoring requirements, adverse effects, and delays related to hospital admission. Most trainees reported insufficient training.
INTERPRETATION: The low response rate (14.8%) and cross-sectional design limit generalisability and causal inference. Self-report bias may overestimate knowledge or understate barriers. While trainees recognise clozapine’s role in TRS, gaps in practical prescribing knowledge and confidence—especially in adverse effect management and monitoring—are evident. The findings suggest a need for structured education and supervised experience, but the study does not evaluate the impact of such interventions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current training may leave trainees underprepared for key aspects of clozapine prescribing. Institutions should consider targeted education and supervised practice to improve confidence and reduce underuse, particularly in areas like adverse effect management and physical health monitoring.

item.title: [14] Intimate partner violence and its association with mental disorders among women in the general population, pregnant women and postpartum women: systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined the association between intimate partner violence (IPV) and mental disorders (depression, anxiety, eating disorders) across three populations: women in the general population, pregnant women, and postpartum women. The study synthesized evidence from cross-sectional, case-control, and cohort studies published between 1980 and 2024.
FINDINGS: The meta-analysis included 82 studies with 140,286 participants. For women in the general population, lifetime IPV was associated with depression (OR 2.26, 95% CI 1.83–2.79). Past-year IPV was linked to depression (OR 2.36, 95% CI 1.61–3.45) and anxiety (OR 2.85, 95% CI 1.61–5.05). Among pregnant women, IPV during pregnancy was associated with depression (OR 3.59, 95% CI 2.48–5.20) and anxiety (OR 3.27, 95% CI 2.60–4.10). For postpartum women, lifetime IPV exposure was associated with depression (OR 2.09, 95% CI 1.54–2.83). The certainty of evidence varied from moderate to very low.
INTERPRETATION: The findings suggest a consistent association between IPV and mental disorders across populations, with stronger associations observed during pregnancy. However, the certainty of evidence is limited by heterogeneity in study designs, populations, and exposure/outcome definitions. The predominance of cross-sectional studies limits causal inference. Confounding by socioeconomic factors or prior mental health conditions may influence the observed associations.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine screening for IPV in psychiatric settings, particularly among pregnant and postpartum women, may be warranted given the elevated risk of depression and anxiety. Clinicians should be aware of the strong associations but interpret findings cautiously due to the low to moderate certainty of evidence. Further high-quality longitudinal research is needed to clarify causality and inform targeted interventions.

item.title: [14] Ketamine for Co-occurring Chronic Pain and Depression: A Scoping Review fing the Dual-Outcome Evidence Gap and Its Treatment and Research Implications.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) examined whether ketamine, an NMDA-receptor antagonist with established antidepressant effects, also improves chronic pain when depressive symptoms are present. It synthesized longitudinal studies assessing both pain and depression outcomes after ketamine treatment, focusing on adults with co-occurring chronic pain and depression.
FINDINGS: Twelve studies (2007–2025) were included: eight with chronic pain populations (≥3 months) and four with primary depression (TRD, MDD, bipolar depression). Most reported concurrent improvements in pain and depressive symptoms. However, only two chronic pain studies used clinical depression diagnoses; others relied on symptom scales. Dosing regimens, study designs, and psychiatric comorbidity varied widely, limiting firm conclusions about ketamine’s dual-action efficacy.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and heterogeneous. The lack of standardized depression ascertainment in chronic pain cohorts and inconsistent pain phenotyping preclude causal inference about ketamine’s analgesic effects in depression. Prospective randomized trials with clinically defined co-occurring chronic pain and depression, standardized dosing, and validated outcome measures are urgently needed to determine efficacy and generalizability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current data suggest possible dual benefit but are insufficient to guide routine use of ketamine for co-occurring chronic pain and depression. Clinicians should await high-quality trials before considering ketamine for this indication, and ensure careful monitoring if used off-label.

item.title: [14] Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists in schizophrenia spectrum disorders: A systematic review and meta-analysis of efficacy, safety and mental health outcomes.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed whether glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) improve psychiatric symptoms, functioning, and safety in adults with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders who are overweight or obese and receiving antipsychotic treatment.
FINDINGS: Six trials (n = 446) were pooled, with only three (n = 102) contributing to the primary psychiatric outcome. Total symptom severity showed an imprecise effect (SMD −0.21, 95% CI −0.60 to 0.19; HKSJ −1.02 to 0.61). Secondary mental health outcomes (functioning, AUDIT, SQLS, BACS) were similarly imprecise, with all confidence intervals crossing the null. GLP-1 RAs significantly reduced body weight (MD −7.42 kg, 95% CI −11.52 to −3.33; I² = 94%), BMI (−2.77 kg/m²), waist circumference (−5.53 cm), and HbA1c (−0.36%). Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent, but serious adverse events were not increased.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence for psychiatric symptom improvement is weak and inconclusive due to small sample sizes, imprecise estimates, and high heterogeneity. The cardiometabolic benefits are more robust but limited by heterogeneity and risk of bias. No conclusions can be drawn regarding cardiovascular outcomes, as these were not assessed. The findings suggest potential utility for weight management but do not support a clear psychiatric benefit.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: GLP-1 RAs may be considered for managing antipsychotic-induced weight gain in schizophrenia, but their impact on psychiatric symptoms remains uncertain. Clinicians should monitor for gastrointestinal side effects and weigh cardiometabolic benefits against limited evidence for mental health improvement.

item.title: [12] Altered effective connectivity during cognitive distancing in cognitive behavioral therapy nonresponders with depression.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study investigated whether pretreatment brain connectivity during cognitive distancing (a key CBT skill) could predict response to CBT in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD). It used fMRI and dynamic causal modeling in 77 outpatients before 25 sessions of CBT as part of the SPeED trial.
FINDINGS: Responders (n=39) showed greater modulation in a dorsomedial-to-ventrolateral prefrontal-to-superior frontal/pre-supplementary motor area network during distancing, while nonresponders had stronger amygdala-to-ventrolateral prefrontal connectivity.
